111 hours and I'm not recommending it. Good God. Pros: Level design, character design, environment art, music: all of these are top-tier and will keep you going throughout a very long journey. Cons: People confuse obfuscation with mystery and bad UX with challenge. To complete this game, you will have to consult a wiki. Not because it is hard (which it is) but because they do very little to tell you where your objectives are. Perhaps they expect you to endlessly wander around the world in hopes you bump into that NPC again. If they put them on the critical path line, maybe that would happen but it is often just in a random spot. That isn't serendipity; it's just being opaque. Maybe the nonsense story would make a bit of sense if information was organized or if there was a basic quest tracker. I don't need a bunch of UI elements to tell me exactly where something is, just try and respect the player a little bit. Did you know that you essentially have to upgrade HP more than any other stat or you will be one-shotted by nearly everything in the game? Would be nice to know, especially since you can only recast your stats halfway-ish through the game. Speaking of respecting the player, if you are going to be tough as nails, you have to be spotlessly bug free. Unfortunately, attacks go through solid objects at random and frame drops will eat your lunch at the worst possible times. There's little joy when you eventually succeed; just relief that an annoying element is done. Luckily, you can often beat bosses by tricking the AI or leveraging a bug in the environment so I guess two can play at that game. And who decided that this game where the character rightly feels like he is wearing forty pounds of armor should be a platformer? I'm happy I roughed my way through it, but I can't see myself recommending it to anyone. It's an interesting game, but not what the incredibly toxic community exalts it as. It's a bleak game with a few truly exquisite moments outweighed by a preponderance of slog. And now I'm finally free of it.

While I did give a yes vote as a recommendation, it comes with a few warnings. This game is NOT made for the PC, it is/was made strictly as a lesser game build for the consoles and it shows. The graphics are not as great as they should be on a PC title. In the first 25 hours the graphical tricks used are obvious and show through the facade of standard console tricks used to help consoles with their performance issues. Another warning is the beyond nonsensical game interface, it was made strictly for a game pad, and it shows. While it is up to the developers to provide proper access and proper ports to the PC, the effort was minimal to the point the PC port of this game is a meme by itself in regards to the keyboard layout and interface choices and key binds. While a huge number of people chime away with "This is a souls title" to wave away the criticism in regards to the poor PC keyboard layout and control options. I do not let these developers off the hook. The keyboard layout and UI suck in a big way. If you do not have a game pad, or do not like to use one, you will be at a disadvantage as there is no assigning any interface controls in a common sense layout. It took me quite a while to get used to the console style approach to minimalist, multi-function buttons in a rotary layout instead of the standard assign whatever action on whatever keystroke freedom I am used to. Another part of the game I do not like is the forced pvp aspect with invasions or the multitude of notes that can be left. The notes clutter the areas, have questionable messages and do nothing for immersion. The invasions, even in a password protected setting is a very stupid choice on the part of the developers. it adds nothing to the game experience and actually degrades the games lore and entertainment values. These things are simply immature carrots for the drop in and drop out crowd and do nothing for the game itself except to let the worst in people ruin an otherwise good game experience. If you want to experience the game without these poorly executed interruptions, play offline, trust me on this. If you are willing to re-learn a bunch of control movements and a very poor UI interface, the game does have a large world and a great challenge with tons of secrets. Though I feel a big part of that challenge is wading through the developers lazy design choices and not the story itself. This game is beautiful, but once I got to the Mountaintops, I stopped being able to appreciate it. Elden Ring's -- like the Dark Souls series before it -- is a combat system built on limitations. Every offensive and defensive option is carried out with either stamina or focus (that is, if you're using magic or ashes of war.) You've also got input buffering to deal with, where button presses have a noticeable delay, and the game registers every input, which WILL lead to accidental panic rolls, drinking flasks one too many times, and doing a mistaken follow-up R2 after doing a jump attack. It's a feature endlessly at odds with the committal controls. You can't cancel your animations, so a good handful of player deaths are a result of people failing to account for an enemy's unavoidable punisher(s) while they're stuck in some animation. This wouldn't be such an issue if enemies didn't all have uniquely rapid combos they can chain together endlessly, and that's on top of everything being way too fast and two-shotting you in the endgame. Not even just bosses, but regular enemies. Many bosses and enemies are simply designed with movesets meant to counter the "few" combat mechanics you have at your disposal. However, I have to say "few" in quotes because there is a wide variety of spells in the game, along with many special attacks you can add to weapons in the form of ashes of war. If you're able to find an effective combination of these things, you can trivialize a lot of the fights, but this solution highlights my main grievance with this game. If something isn't working, you're not meant to adapt to an enemy until it does. You're meant to trivialize the shit by min-maxing. That kind of stuff may be fun for PVP, but, unless they're an invader, enemies don't play by the same rules you do. All of this wouldn't be such a problem if there were another angle to the gameplay, but fighting your way through the world is the only thing your character is good for, sadly. And that's a real shame when you have such cool a setting with so many major characters. Imagine pledging fealty to a Shardbearer with a kneel emote in the middle of battle or something, and then you get to join their faction instead of just killing every single one of them. That's the kind of shit I play RPGs for, but all you get here are fragmented questlines you need spoilers just to complete, and omniscient item descriptions. My final note: I know nothing of the game's community or meta or what-have-you, but if the only way I can enjoy or beat a game is by looking up everything and playing it someone else's way, then the game just ain't for me. And on the off-chance you're anything like me, then it probably ain't for you either.

[b] At the time of writing, I have beaten Elden Ring seven times, almost beaten it an eighth time, and achieved 100% completion in terms of Steam achievements. This is a good game. A great game. But it's held back from being perfect by a couple things. [/b] Elden Ring is one of the most solid games ever created, and rivals the rest of the FromSoftware catalogue for best title they've ever created. The problem is, Elden Ring seems to have taken a tip from the original Dark Souls by making the second half of the game filled with unnecessary difficulty spikes, that make the game less fun and more frustrating than challenging. One such example of this is a section in the optional area of the [spoiler] 'Consecrated Snowfield' [/spoiler], this section is known as [spoiler] 'Ordina, Litgurgical Town' [/spoiler]. In this section there seems to be a lack of thought in the design, and it pairs the weakest part of these games - the platforming - with archer enemies placed in hard to reach positions that fire both very quick, and very fast. Alongside this, there are invisible assassin enemies who can crit you and then go invisible once more, leaving only a small window to actually hit them. Another example of this difficulty, and what I consider the main one, is the bosses - the bosses in the second half seem to have too much health, and deal too much damage, with almost all of them after [spoiler] Morgott [/spoiler] being able to 1 to 3 hit you depending on your build. This, I do not find challenging, just completely unfair; the worst offender is by far [spoiler] The Fire Giant [/spoiler] who might be the most infuriating mainline boss From has ever created. On the other hand, this title is the most expansive, most open and offers the most diverse build variety of any of the titles that FromSoft have created before. I also think this is among one of its most polished titles, which is why the unnecessary difficulty in certain sections makes it so frustrating as a title. Why bring down the quality of this game by designing unfair, and thus unenjoyable sections in a near perfect title? I think it has something to do with the legacy that FromSoftware has left behind with their souls-like genre; that of the idea that a souls-like must be difficult. This in turn can sometimes result in artificial difficulty over real challenge in order to make the game fit this image of being a 'difficult game'. However, I must whole-heartedly recommend this title, as it's easily one of the best games I've ever played, and probably will ever play.

[H1]So what's it about?[/H1] You are are revived and you find yourself in the Lands Between. Embarking on an epic quest you will need to find and to do what it takes to become and Elden Lord. [H1]The good[/H1] The visuals, sound and music are stunning. The world building is great: there are so many locations to explore, so many secrets to discover and the monster design never gets boring. And then when you have thought you saw everything you are thrown in another big adventure. There are optional areas in the game that you may just walk by because you don't realize they are there. There are bosses and mini-bosses that you will not see unless you look for them. It brings you back to how games used to be: explore and find new things without everything being served on a plate to you. Being able to complete the game and then realize the game wasn't serving you all the content but instead you need to discover it is great. The multiplayer portion is similar to Death Stranding where other players can leave you messages and you can see little blood spots where other players died. It's also cool to see the ghosts of others moving through the world and of course you can PvP if you want if you have the correct items. It's a good thing to fully integrate this in the game as prevent you from feeling lonely. There is some PVE and PVP and with the right items equipped you can select what you would like to do. The items and equipment that you can find is absolutely amazing: even more when you realize that there are no DLCs, microtransactions or other schemes. You pay what you get and it works. I wish other games were still like that. [H1]The not so good[/H1] The difficulty can be punishing at times - it's part of the charm of the game / series but you might get frustrated because you feel it's unfair. You will need to build your character and get to understand the game mechanics or the bosses will make quick work of you. Without the right tactics you will die a lot regardless whether you are a high level or not. It can be frustrating but all it means you are not good enough - level up, practise, get better and rethink your tactics :-). You will need to use a gamepad to play this game. I cannot see how you can play this with mouse and keyboard. I used a Switch Pro Controller and that worked great. While not experiencing bugs or system issues I got several disconnects from the multiplayer part because of "Inappropriate Activity Detected, Unable to Start in Online Mode". I have no idea what happened here as I was just riding my horse at those times. Usually after 10 - 15 minutes I was able to logging back on. There are many extended quests in the game. You will not realize this at first as there is no quest book, tracker or even on-screen notification. As you can kill NPCs you may lose their story lines without even realizing it. You will have to make choices but there is not really a good or bad one so it's much how you want to role play. Because of this system as you may like to explore a lot you will find that quests have moved on: NPCs moved to a different location than you expected or you just don't realize there was a quest at all. This can be a bit annoying at times especially when you have play sessions every few days. It's hard to get back on track without making lots of notes. The marker system on the map only allows 100 bookmarks but there are so many more areas to explore. I wish the limit was raised as in the end I had to keep track of my progress in a notepad. Very much how I used to play old style games. Why can't we turn off chromatic aberration? I know there is a mod but I didn't want to play my first play through using a mod. Your character cannot swim or climb I loved that in Zelda Breath of the Wild or Assassin's Creed and I wish we could do it here as well. There are many, many systems in the game that you find or miss. Basically, you can upgrade just about everything but you need to find the right location, NPC and items. The game will do little to hold your hand it's up to you to discover. [H1]Summary[/H1] I enjoyed my journey through the Lands Between so far and I will definitely return. It was tough at times but it felt like a breath of fresh air. The visuals and audio are some of the best, I have ever seen. The world building is amazing and I enjoyed all the secrets that I found but also that I learned there is even more to find. Hopefully other developers will study what Elden Ring does well and learn from it as it sets a new milestone for open world gaming.

Elden Ring is definitely my game of the year for 2022. Took me about 220 hours and three playthroughs to get 100% achievements and was worth the time. There is so much to do, you never get bored. As per From Software's history, the story is obscure but rewards exploring. There are also a variety of ways to play. You can play as a hack and slash type, sword and board, pure spellcaster, or some unique combination that fits your gear or play-style.

Despite the open-world singleplayer RPG genre continually devolving into pointless fetch quests, poorly written dialogue, and excessive hand-holding, Elden Ring stands out by doing everything exactly how other games don't - and it works beautifully. This is essentially my first Souls game. I very briefly played DS3, and barely played Sekiro, so I began Elden Ring with an open mind and virtually no expectations. I assumed I'd be in for an interesting, combat centric pseudo-RPG that would be confusing and frustrating. That's what I got, however for some reason, despite initial frustrations with difficulty, the overload of information that is the stats screen, and the complete lack of guidance in what to do, Elden Ring is absurdly captivating. The environments are varied and gorgeous, dungeons are clearly crafted with care and attention to detail, and characters are interesting (lovable sort ahead). This is the first game that has had me absolutely and entirely immersed since some of my all-time favourite single-player experiences such as Fallout: New Vegas or Skyrim. The Lands Between is an expanse packed to the brim with fun content, interesting loot, and once you start exploring you never want to stop. The questlines are interesting (though you'll definitely need some help from Fextralife), and the boss fights are straight up epic. The music is downright beautiful and the visuals are so unique, so stylized, and so gorgeous in so many different ways. I have tried to write and rewrite this review for months, and every time, I feel dissatisfied with my own ability to convey exactly how much this game has blown me away. But now, I think I've found the perfect way to put it: I put down Elden Ring after playing non-stop, clocking almost 300 hours. Wanting to scratch my open world RPG itch, I revisited Witcher 3 and put in a cool 70 hours then put it down for a reason I couldn't understand. So I put together a new Skyrim modlist, spent probably 30 hours modding and troubleshooting and then another 30 playing, then put it down for a reason I couldn't understand. Hogwarts Legacy came out, and despite my love for the Harry Potter universe, for some reason I couldn't even push myself to finish the main story. I finally relented, and came to terms with the fact that I'd just rather be playing this game. Elden Ring is a masterpiece. It is an undeniable champion amongst a stale genre saturated with mediocrity and tired franchises. It is a tour de force, a chef d'ouvre, a pièce de résistance. Yes, I pulled up a thesaurus. Could this be a dog?

Elden Ring is the culminative mastering of Fromsoft's design for the past decade on top of treading new grounds in the form of an open world with horizontal progression compared to past games which were much more linear in design. It is unabashedly masterful in execution; it feels like the Soulsborne series was always meant to reach this. By far this is the game where it is the easiest to get into; progression gating is very limited, most of the map is accessible without the need to defeat bosses. There is a plethora of play-styles that are viable; Miracle builds are now finally made viable, its on that level. The Spirit Ashes add a new option for solo play that's more available for players to use. The story feels much more cohesive and fleshed out than any previous Fromsoft game that I have experienced. Not going to drop spoilers, but its amazing how things feel connected as you progress through the story. There are a few prominent pain points. There is some reusing of bosses, which in an open world game is perfectly fine, however there are instances where they are poorly placed, such as two different instances of a boss enemy with different movesets in a small arena, which makes the encounter feel arbitrarily difficult. There are a few enemies that are less than enjoyable to fight as well, and there is a big difficulty spike in the later areas. However these are relatively minor flaws that can be circumvented. Elden Ring feels like a childhood dream of adventure. Its easy to lose yourself to the adventure. Take it from me; game already ate up 100+ hours in the first week. To the veterans of the Soulsborne games, this is a worthwhile purchase. To the newcomers, this is probably the best first game for the series, it will take some learning but if you really want to get into souls games, this is one.

As a long time fan of Fromsoftware's modern output, Elden Ring has easily became my favorite next to Sekiro (though, you can't really compare these two). I'm not going really dwell on each aspect of the game as a whole, so I'm just going to say some helpful tips: * PERFORMANCE Performance isn't really good, but it goes away after a while and by the time I went deeper into the game it was for the most part resolved. It does leave a bad first impression though sadly, and I'm generally disappointed at Fromsoftware for this, but in the end I kind of forgot about it since it really starts to go away after a while (it's classic shader stutter apparently). If this is really upsetting but you do want to keep playing, here are some tips: - Try going offline, it doesn't help much, but it's worth a shot - If you have enough memory, try setting shader cache to a higher value in your GPU setting After a while it's easy for the game to lock on 40-50 in the open world and 60 in dungeons on recommended specs, but I won't say that this is ideal, it's easily the weakest aspect of the game. * GAMEPLAY TIPS If you are yet to play the game, here are my tips that I think can improve your experience (especially if this is your first Fromsoftware game): - Pay absolutely no attention to the "Meta", meta is the enemy of fun. It's quite easy to build really high damage builds in this game, especially towards the end. Just pick up something that you like for early to mid-game. You do need to at least somewhat prioritize higher damage in the end-game though, but by that time, you'll probably have more than enough tools on your hand. - There are quite a few multi-enemy bosses in the game. Don't treat them like O&S in Dark Souls, they were clearly never designed with the intention of you fighting them solo (which is a shame really). Summon a spirit, and if you do want to keep things "fair", remember that you can summon your spirit back by using the same item for summoning after the fight becomes one on one. Remember that spirits are an actual part of your build, rather than just some tools on the side. Once again, forget the meta, use whatever you like. - Also on spirit summons, if you think that your summon is "stealing the fight" from you, there is talisman called "Shabriri's Woe" that you can get early game. Put that on, and the boss will prioritize you over your summon. It's surprising how well the summons can support you this way, while keeping you in control of the fight. - Have multiple weapons with varying levels of upgrade. The game showers you with upgrade material just by clearing the major dungeons, and most of your damage comes from upgrade level instead of your stats. As long as you have the minimum stats and the correct infusion on the weapon, you'll have a pretty reliable weapon on hand. The reason that I suggest this is that it's quite easy to miss major areas and become over-leveled for those areas. Of course, the game has no problem with you destroying bosses, but if you do want a challenge, switch to a lower upgrade weapon, that'll be more than enough to level the field. Beyond that, it's just fun having multiple weapons to use in this game. - Horse combat is almost completely optional to engage in. There are fights that I personally think are much more enjoyable with the horse, but there is no force on you to do that. If you do end up using the horse, I recommend you use a halberd or a long weapon. Short weapons just don't work on your horse if you are moving fast (at least I couldn't make them work). - Don't sleep on the Ash of War system. Some of them are really useful. You can make entire playthroughs around some of these ashes (like the magical parry thingy ... or the one that restores your health when you hit someone). The infusion also means that you can use many weapon classes effectively. This is quite different from Dark Souls or Bloodborne, you really aren't bound to a class of weapons based on your build, and the game I will go as far to say, expects you to roleplay as different builds frequently. - The crafting system isn't really that much in depth, but some of the consumables like Volcano Pots can completely melt some enemies; It's really funny. Give it a try once, if it doesn't interest you, then just forget it exists ... - Invest at least a *bit* in Faith. Like maybe up to 12 or 15. Some incantations serve only defensive purposes, and are extremely useful in the end game, when the enemy damage becomes ridiculous. If not for that, just take a look at Lake of Rot ... you'll thank me later. - On topic of defense, this is the first time I think your armor actually matters. Not only in the end game, but even as early as mid game, you can start getting chunked for like half your health quite easily if you are not careful. So either wear good armor, or use defensive talismans. - There are a few "holes" on the map that the game gives you (like little brown circles ...), make sure you check them out. They are mines that usually always have bell bearings that you can trade in the hub for infinite supply of upgrade materials. Don't miss them. Hope these help

I always found the Souls games to be a bit inaccessible, but Elden Ring was the first time I really "got" what is special about the genre and about From Software. The unique world, with lore as deep as you care to delve, full of brilliant design and art direction, makes Elden Ring stand out as uniquely enticing among a sea of same-y open world games. There are no quest arrows or compasses, and minimal hand-holding in general; a refreshing harkening back to a time when RPGs didn't focus on being streamlined as much as they did on being immersive. Everything has an exciting air of mystery. You have to explore in Elden Ring, and it doesn't feel like a chore or a distraction or a time sink standing in the way of getting to the good stuff. None of the content here feels like filler. (The vast majority of it is optional, in fact. Side quests are not afterthoughts, they're the core of the experience.) Exploration is rewarding here. It's what you'll want to do as you play, and the game's design philosophy is all about encouraging it, letting the player mostly direct their own journey. Combat can be difficult, yes, but also rewarding and deep, offering tons of build options where most things feel viable and nothing feels particularly obligatory. Most of what turned me off about the souls-like genre before, was not wanting to reach a sticking point and becoming frustrated with my inability to advance. Elden Ring is full of challenging bosses that you may bang your head against, but the open and non-linear nature of the game means you always have some other content you can go do instead if you get stuck on a particular encounter. Leveling up and finding better gear is basically always an option. Elden Ring challenges, and can sometimes frustrate, but never quite enough to keep you away. And the feeling of accomplishment when you are successful is all the sweeter. It's clear when you play that for the game's creators, this was a labor of love. It's not perfect, but what flaws it has are easy to overlook in face of it's many virtues. If you're like me and you're apprehensive about it because of the Souls genre's reputation for difficulty and high skill floor, do yourself a favor and take the chance on this one. You may surprise yourself, and this game will probably surprise you.

This is the Dark Souls II that FromSoft WANTED to make, as opposed to the one we actually got. It has many of the same annoyances—gank-heavy enemy placements, questionable hitboxes, a lot of fights seemingly being designed with only one strategy in mind—but it also corrects many of the worst aspects of DS2, and you actually get an entire continent to explore instead of a convolution of impossible spaces. If you liked DS2, you'll probably like ER—and if you didn't like DS2, as I and so many others didn't, there's still a very good chance you'll like ER anyway. It's not a perfect game. The open world GENERALLY avoids feeling boring and empty like in many other open-world games—but some areas still feel like a slog. Enemy strength scales by area, just like in Dark Souls, not according to your level or equipment, which makes exploring some areas a bit more frustrating, but you can always hop on Torrent for a quick getaway—though that only applies to certain definitions of "quick," because Torrent feels like the slowest horse in video games and turns like a boot. Still, he can double-jump, which allows for some interesting routes. All in all, though, this is the best Soulslike I've played. I didn't think I'd like it better than DS1, but it exceeded my expectations. But this long after it came out, are you really still looking at reviews to decide whether you want to buy it?

Ignore the hype, ignore you're friends, don't bother playing this game. REQUIRES AT LEAST 10 hours of tutorial videos on builds, basic game mechanics, and side quests that exist in the game before actually playing. The game does not teach you anything about how to play it, you need to rely on outside help in order to progress. This includes basic things like how to navigate the menu, how to create a strong character, which weapons to use, etc. The difficulty curve is set up so that you NEED to learn these things early on, else you will not progress in the game. To start off, here is the entire plot to the game: you want to be elden lord, maybe. That's it. Some characters are more or less keen on that, but it's not really clear. Most of the lore and "story" of the game can be found in item descriptions, and its the most ineffectual way to tell a story that I have ever encountered. Side missions have zero logic to them, basically you need to talk to every NPC in the game in order to progress a mission without referencing a guide or tutorial. Most missions have a point where you grab some item like "the sacred toenail of Ira the dancer" and for some reason you are supposed to know that "Ephesius" needs that to make it to Narnia or some nonsense like that. Many of these side missions are necessary to beat the game at a reasonable difficulty level, else you will be under leveled or poorly equipped to face required bosses. Honestly I can't talk about this game without referencing the menu, it is the most poorly organized, laziest feature to any video game I have ever played. This studio has had an entire decade to hone the menuing system in their RPG game, and the best thing they can come up with is a literal grab bag of items organized like a pile of clothes on a teenagers dorm room floor. I cannot tell you how many times I grabbed an item only to never use it in my play-through simply because I lost it in the menu. There is a lantern in this game, and I have to play Where's Waldo every single time I try to equip it simply because I picked something up on the ground in an open world RPG game, and it reshuffled my items. Gameplay wise, its a souls game. That is to say, its a rhythm game that tries to cheese you every step of the way. In some ways, I find this rewarding, especially when facing groups of enemies in the games various dungeons. Assuming you have min/maxed your character to make the fight doable of course. Most of these encounters are well set up to challenge you to figure out a strategy to beat them consistently, given limited space and resources. Unfortunately, this is an open world game, and the majority of encounters occur in the open world. In these cases, it is easy to bypass encounters by going around them, or fighting them one on one. To make up for that, the game designers added lots of harder enemies that are required fights for one reason or another. All of these fights devolve into "big guy with sword in field" or "big guy with axe in field", and have basically the same move sets. The best way to deal with them is to grind levels until you can easily combo or one shot them, otherwise you're in for repetitive, uninspired fights. A majority of enemies are direct copy pastes of one another, and it's a shame. It's a shame because the art might be the best I have seen in a video game. There are many biomes/areas to explore, and each their own unique artistic style to them. You can easily tell which area you are in just by the art style of the world around you. I visited every single area in this game simply because I wanted to explore the environment that the artists created, and I put up with all of repetitive gameplay and the obnoxious bosses to do it. The bosses in this game suffer the same issue as the enemies. At least half are re-used throughout the game, the worst example being used at least 6 times. Many of them share similar move-sets as well, making the artistically unique bosses seem like copies of earlier ones. Put simply, fighting them is a chore. The bigger, "demigod" bosses are more unique, at least early in the game. But more often than not, they can only be defeated by a "normal" player by cheesing them. Multiple times in this game I have been impressed by a boss design, only to realize the best way to defeat them is an unsatisfying cheese that the game gives you as an apology for making their boss unbeatable at the level you are supposed to face them. Towards the end of the game, it becomes a boss rush, and there are no more cheese strategies available. In order to beat these, you need to enter into an hours long gameplay loop of getting one shot to each combo they throw out so you can learn the precise moment you need to dodge in order to avoid their attacks. If you grind hard enough, you can eventually see the ending to a game with zero story. I played this game because a friend recommended it. They said they enjoyed it, and they hoped I did too, and then apologized for telling me I should play it. Many people on here have the same story, and many of their friends say they enjoyed the game as well. The only explanation I can come up with is that this game is Type 2 fun. When you are in the moment, playing the game, its terrible. Once you are done, and you've completed it, the feeling of accomplishment you get overshadows those moments of frustration, the monotony of grinding, and the times you left the game defeated. You commiserate with your friends, and it becomes a shared experience that you can connect with. Eventually you forget the negative feelings you had while playing the game, and the memories that persist are those of the adventure you embarked on, and the feeling of growth that came out of it. But when I play this game, I can't help but wonder what I actually am supposed to get out of it. I pressed dodge the exact millisecond I needed to five times in a row, and won a boss encounter because of it. Was that worth it? Is practicing this one button press for an hour straight really what I'm doing with my time? More than anything, thing game makes me question why I spend time playing it instead of doing something else. The first encounter in Elden Ring is with a hulking mass of thrashing bodies, congealed in a spider like blob of legs and arms. If it is your first playthrough, it easily dispatches you with a few swipes of its relatively tiny sword, shrugging off any damage you attempt to inflict. Veteran players, expecting the monster, can beat it with well timed dodges and strikes, though it is no easy feat. The reward for doing so is a short walk to a nearby pathway, where the ground gives out, killing you instantly. The same can be said for the game as a whole. No matter what you do, the end result is the same, you get nothing for your time, your energy, your frustration. In the end, it is a futile waste of effort. Go read a book instead.

Oh, Elden Ring! *Small spoiler warning for boss names* Absolutely brimming with great content, Elden Ring surpassed my unhealthily high expectations. As a veteran of the series, I was very hyped for ER (probably too much), yet the game still blew me away. The small dungeons were what I was most worried about. Most games of ER's size tend to re-use dungeons, and while some of them feel samey, they were clearly made with a lot of effort. Their difficulty progresses very well throughout the game, and the late game ones are worth every minute of exploration. The bosses are outstanding, but Dark Souls 3 and Bloodborne are still (in my opinion, this is very subjective) the games with the best fights in the series. Elden Ring's best bosses have minor flaws which make them just a bit more annoying than enjoyable. To give examples: Malenia's damage output and Waterfowl dance; Mohg's bloodflame covering the entire arena, making bloodloss unavoidable if you're too unlucky; Rykard's nearly unavoidable exploding skulls; Placidusax's huge health bar that makes the fight an endurance test like no other; and so on. However, don't get me wrong: All of these bosses are still very fun. These flaws are minor annoyances. The music is truly outstanding, and I have nothing negative to say about it. Morgott, Mohg, Malenia, Placidusax, The Godskin Apostles, and many more amazing tracks are among the series' best. The graphics are nothing revolutionary, but the art style is unforgettable. There is a geoguessr game for ER (lostgamer.io), but all the locations are so distinct from one another that it's very easy to guess them all just from a single playthrough. Boss designs, area designs, everything is so full of life that you wonder how they managed to make it all in 5 years. Conclusion: one of the best games ever made, well worth the money, and then some. Fingers crossed that FromSoftware will keep up the tradition of making the DLC the most epic and over the top (in a good way) experience in gaming history.

I love the game but i just have one problem with it, dont get me wrong its an amazing experience and i really recomend it. But since its open world and you can get almost every weapon in the game when you start or shortly after it feels a lot easier than the other souls-games.

THE GOOD: * New open world setting. This works phenomenally, the change from the cramped and claustrophobic gauntlets in older Fromsoft titles to open plains in the Lands Between feels amazing. The freedom of engaging the world at your own pace is such a wonderful introduction. The areas introduced all feel unique with it's own stories to tell. *A fantastic, intricate and engaging lore. How can we describe the story and lore of Elden Ring? Well, I'd say Early Christianity, western alchemy, Gnosticism, occultism and mysticism. The historical foundation that serves as a base for the game's storytelling has been greatly expanded compared to earlier titles and is now bigger than ever. This makes this game such a joy to unravel, puzzling together the historical references. *Stunning and unparalleled visuals This game offers some of the most stunning colors, weathers and atmospheres I've seen in a game. Each zone has it's own unique climate, flora and color palette that it nails perfectly. From the ever-clouded plains of Limgrave, the starry skies of Liurnia to the snowy mountaintop of the Giants. THE BAD: *The game sadly plays too much like an older Dark Souls game And what I mean by this, despite Elden Ring's adaptation to a more modern open world RPG, it still plays out like the titles of yore. It's a railroaded boss slaying game that offers very limited effects of player choices and world interactions. Many NPCs questlines feature interesting early stages that can be skipped altogether (Rogier, Ranni etc), without any punishment or loss of valuable items. It makes the game feel extremely streamlined as it doesn't reward thorough gameplay more akin to a RPG. *Limited weapon and armor variety My favorite thing about Dark Souls 3 was the absolute variety of gear in the world. Soldiers and knights in the Lands Between all carry more or less identical gear. The pinhead knight armor having the same model across all factions is disappointing. Not to mention they all wield the exact same weapons. The Brass Shield, the Lordsworn Straight- and Greatsword, Knight's Greatsword and Partisan. A world filled with different heritages and traditions should enable a more diverse selection of styles. *Low enemy variety This somewhat follows in the same track as the previous one, just as we see a lack of variety of gear on enemies, we also have a lack of variety when it comes to enemies. What truly makes an area feel unique is it's denizens. Sadly, as we progress to the later stages of the game we can really notice how the enemy variety fizzles out, and in the final zones of the game we end up fighting more or less the same enemies we've fought before, but now they have a lot more HP, defense and attack. That's it. *Unfinished and cut content "First you should do when you're done writing, is rewriting" Anyone who followed the initial announcement of Elden Ring probably expected what a rollercoaster the development process must've been. Ultimately, we ended up with a game worthy of the GOTY title, but in the end we can't help but notice how certain things feel missing or incomplete. A cross comparison of item descriptions from the 1.00 version of the game reveals fundamentally different lore implications. A plethora of NPCs and questlines have been cut and reworked (Kale and the Great Caravan is one example), and we cannot know for sure what impact that might have had on the original vision of the game. Will these be reworked and reintroduced in expansions? Perhaps, but remember these were NPCs that were supposed to be in the base game (looking at you Rico). This was my first From Software Souls game and I absolutely did not expect to enjoy this as much as I did. I have some gripes with it but overall this was one of the best RPGs I've ever played. First, a few negatives; As my first Souls game I had no idea what I was doing for the first few hours of the game and I had to constantly rely on YouTube as my companion. The tutorial at the start of the game was pretty bare bones, I didn't even realise you could run until a few hours in. The difficulty was extremely punishing at the start of the game. For returning players I imagine this isn't a problem as the mechanics transfer from previous games, but for me I had a hard time until a few YouTube videos taught me the basics. After you get over the initial hurdle you learn that the game rewards patience, it's all about learning the enemies attack patterns and punishing them when they show an opening. Although the world itself is magnificent and the enemy variety and design were great, the game really sucks at telling a cohesive story. I had no idea what was going on and what my motivations were through a lot of the game. And my final complaint... no ultra wide support, that sucks on a game this big. As negative as that all sounded, I still think this was one of the best games I've ever played. It's so satisfying learning the attack patterns of a boss and then trying again and again until you defeat them. The open world was huge and there was always something interesting to find. You'll constantly be sidetracked by branching pathways on your way to a destination. The loot almost always felt rewarding, and even when I was deep into the game I was still finding new areas and mechanics. The ability to spec your character to whatever you preferred play style is great. The enemies were always interesting, some of the bosses had the coolest designs. The art and music were blended together perfectly. I've completed the main story and I think I've been to every main area of the map but I'm sure there's still hours of content in the game for me should I choose to explore further. I'm glad I gave this game a chance. It won game of the year for a reason.

I don't really know what to say. This game is a mixed bag for me. On the one hand, I don't like this game. It's too big. The side dungeons/caves/catacombs are all half-baked and don't add much to the game. I feel the game is simultaneously too easy AND too hard. It suffers from a lack of focus and I think doesn't do a good job at making travelling from point to point interesting. Again, I really think the game is far too big. Remove the side content entirely and focus on making more legacy dungeon content/ actually interesting open-world engagements, and it'd be much, much better in my eyes. On the other hand... God. This game changed my life. I don't know what it is, but I find myself appreciating life more, appreciating the things I have, and have gained a deeper understanding of what I even look for in life. A bit dramatic, sure? But I'm a very emotional person. I can't really describe my feelings without turning this review into a dissertation, so I'll keep it brief. Elden Ring showed me that things are beautiful in spite of all the ugly things around it. And it taught me to appreciate what I have, and not to force things to be the same just because they feel good. I love playing this game with my friends. The issues I have still exist, and I think the way that co-op is handled does not fit the nature of an open-world game. I prefer the Seamless Co-Op mod for this reason. I feel as if Seamless is the way the game is meant to be played as far as co-op goes (even if the Rot mechanic is stupid as fuck. The game is hard enough already.) I dunno. I guess I recommend it? It would feel disingenuous to not recommend it after the effect it's had on me. I guess I should just say: Temper your expectations going in. Don't buy into the hype. Don't focus too much on what other people have to say. Just make it your own experience.

Honestly this game is incredibly overrated. Story is super vague and uninteresting, and combat is incredibly frustrating. It's just memorizing movesets and not making a mistake. I can see why this is "the best soulsborne" but that doesn't make it game of the year. What a waste of money. I'll keep rage-playing this just so no one can say I didn't give it a chance and I just need to git gud, but I swear I'll update when I've beat the game that it's still bad. The super punishing boss fights are fun because they're bosses. I will give the game that. I like Monster Hunter, I like Remnant, I like bosses that are really hard. They're incredibly cheap and purposefully designed so, but they're right on the edge of punishing and too cheap, and they're bosses so fine. But for miniboss types or exploring the story path, the basic design of this game is really annoying. If you die when you get to a new enemy type, which you will, CONSTANTLY, then you have to wade through a bunch of mooks who can kill you in three shots by stunlocking you with a buddy, and congrats, now you've lost all the runes you had on your fucking corpse retrieval. Who does corpse retrievals still in 2022? So to get to the new enemy you have to play perfectly just to get another shot, but they are all designed with incredibly unpredictable movesets with halting, unnatural moves so you can't predict when to block or dodge. The whole game concept feels like that mario maker video where every time mario jumps an invisible hazard pops out as an F you. F you, you had no way of knowing this would happen, but now you do. So go back and if you successfully predict that move, awesome, he's got branching paths off the same stance that have equally unpredictable moves. I don't understand why people think dying a ton in order to learn a moveset is fun. And again, the moves are designed to be unpredictable. You can't learn your skills and get good at the game and get better, you have to learn each individual enemy type. And it's not just the mechanics of combat that has bad cues, the rest of the game does too. The giant tree knight at the beginning is way too hard to fight. Ok, I understand that after a try or two, but the tutorial, the dude you talk to at the beginning, the tip screens, no one says "hey, you need to be careful, don't try to kill everything." There are no hints that the bigger something is, the more dangerous it is. There are no hints that if you get stuck, you should go screw around somewhere else and level up, then come back. ALL of that has to be learned through internet research (bad design) or banging your head against the wall so you're frustrated and now have a sour taste in your mouth after owning the game for a few hours. Even like exploring, the game tells you explicitly to follow the glowing paths, but if you do so you'll be incredibly underleveled. So not only do you need to explore the whole section of the map you uncover, you need to go off into gray unexplored sections as well. ALL of this is counter to standard game design and gamer instincts. That doesn't make the game original and inventive, it makes it bad because it doesn't tell you any of that. It's a choose your own adventure book that says "make sure to read the story" and doesn't mention you can skip around. I legitimately don't understand how this game has mass appeal. For fans of the genre, sure, absolutely. But a game of the year should transcend genre. A truly amazing game is at least fun to play for a while even if you're not a fan of the genre. I feel like I'm taking crazy pills when people talk about the wide appeal of this game.

That alone is enough to keep me playing the game for hours, I definitely feel like I have gotten my money's worth. I have logged 900 hours on playstation as well as these 153 on PC. after the work they put into it on PC it runs much better and I encounter very little issues. If I really had to pick something to list as a con (and this is some deep nit picking) I suppose it would be the grass rendering. I only recommend this game for it's adventure; exploration and beauty is unparalleled and cannot match any other soulslike. However, it's combat is simultaneously a repeat of old soulslikes but done in the worst way possible. The beauty of the soulslike combat system was one-on-one combat: attack, dodge, and parry. Keeping perfect time and rhythm. This game doesn't have rhythm or timing. Just constant barrages of attacks from every single enemy barring the largest and most awkward. You will feel under pressure every second but never a chance to retaliate except for only in the most minute openings. From Software's games have certainly felt the pressure of being "Difficult" and are being pressed to take it's formula and press it to it's logical maxima until it no longer resembles the original. These enemies and bosses do not feel like they are from the original or from any soulslike that has come out since, but enemies from non soulslike games. Games where the player should be able to return with equal force, but never can because they feel like they themselves are ripped from DS1. This game will never reach the infamy of DS2 but so many encounters encompass what made that game more frustrating than fun: ambushes and memorization. Great hard games test reaction times not memorization, like the difference between the first and second Halo Legendary campaigns: where the second involved little reaction and plenty of memory after first failing many many times, the first always presented you with tests of skill for things you've previously gone through, clearly presenting the danger up front and allowing thought for your next moves for every encounter. The first Halo respected the player and wanted them to win, it understood it was a game and while it challenged the player it did not provide a wall that required narrow windows and laugh at you for not finding them. Elden Ring feels like the Dungeon Master that hated their players, the teacher that wanted you to fail, or the backstabbing friend that never was on your side. If this was not a game then I would recommend it beyond exploring, if learning software engineering was a game I wouldn't recommend it, if learning art was a game I wouldn't recommend it, if being alive was a game I wouldn't recommend it. It doesn't matter how hard the anything is, you will eventually get good enough at to beat it. When people complain about souls games, they're not having fun. Its not because it's hard. TL;DR/Bottom Line: The game is only kind of fun, but if every hobby, and almost every other game bores you, then you may find this game thoroughly fun after the exploration runs out.

You can go anywhere you wish but you will have to figure things on your own. To some people its exactly what they want, and for some it would be a terrible experience. Things you will experience: - 1) Beautiful Landscapes 2) Sense of true exploration 3) Frustration (because the game is designed to be hard and is unforgiving, but you will get used to it). 4) Epic feeling/sense of accomplishment once you beat a certain boss. 5) Little to no happiness, dark world. Things elden ring need to have for me to give it 10/10 1) Easy mode - It enables casual gamers to have a lore experience and not grind for an hour to learn boss patterns to beat them, it might be something a souls fan would love but a casual gamer is not looking to experience that. They just want to experience the art of the game and lore. 2) Game mechanics/rules need to be fair for everyone in the game - For eg In elden ring you cannot cancel your animation, but some bosses do not respect it. (Malenia) and every spell should have some cooldown to it to prevent npc from constantly spamming it due to error in programming. 3) A guide (Yes a guide) - As mentioned in point 1, the majority of gamers play games casually. So a guide system would be helpful (something like questhelper from World of Warcraft). It can try to guide a player for a more linear progression. 4) Option to re-fight a boss - Personally when I finished the game, I wanted to fight certain bosses because those were fun. But unfortunately you cannot and the only option is the new game+, I don't feel like doing the same again just to fight bosses. Especially when I have already finished 100% of the game. There is no incentive in doing so when you have already explored the whole game. 5) True coop: I don't know how can such a beautiful game have such a bad co-op experience, it has been solved upto some extend by modding community when they created "Seamless co-op". But true co-op in elden ring would have made it 100x better in my opinion. Overall, the game is gonna give you a great experience. Go for it! :)

Most games are rollercoaster rides that guide you from one point to the next while trying to keep your attention through exposition that rarely amounts to anything more than popcorn. While there is nothing wrong with that and said games can provide entertainment, the overall experience tends to be forgettable. Elden Ring takes the established Souls formula and puts it in a Zelda like open world. After 500+ hours I still find new stuff, uncover dialogue with NPCs, etc. While all the elements to keep you entertained for hours upon hours are there, there is also a lot more. It's like a digital painting, a work of art. From the colour palette to the music. Even though the world is a bleak, surreal and dreamy nothing feels out of place. Every item, NPC, piece of dialogue feels like it belongs there for a reason. This unfortunately isn't always true for the side content, which is one of drawbacks of an open world. The obvious shortcomings of an open world game are easily overlooked by the overall experience that is present here. It makes the Souls formula accessible to a larger mainstream audience without handicapping the experience or the artistic narrative. Elden Ring will undoubtedly go down as a masterpiece along fondly remembered titles like Grim Fandango or Deus Ex.

There's very few ways I could talk about this game that are unique or interesting, because enough ink's been spilled that even reviewing it feels trite. I've been following Fromsoft games for the better part of a decade, starting with buying Demon's Souls way back in 2011, just before Dark Souls dropped on the PS3. So I'll start by stealing words from someone who's smarter than I am, specifically Noah Caldwell-Gervais: "Elden Ring is not a perfect game, but it is idiosyncratic, which is almost as good and just as rare." It's pretty remarkable that From Software's brand of animation timing-based combat, meticulous level design and striking art direction and tone not only translates to the open world format but even makes it truly worthwhile and interesting. The map is huge, but I still know its peaks and valleys, sheer cliff faces and miserable swamp lands like the back of my hand; I was concerned that the expansion of scope would mean it would be harder to get an idea of the layout of the Lands Between just because of its sheer breadth. That's not the case because its layout is still every bit as crafted as any other fromsoft map. Sheer cliff faces from a map that dares you to traverse its landscape, jagged rock like fingers reaching out, as though the land itself wants to grab you, swallow you whole. I've never seen an open world so fearlessly use its verticality to limit the player's exploration and force you to find a way around. Sure there are games with taller skyscrapers, bigger mountains, but there's a difference between something being tall and something feeling tall. You can take an elevator to the top floor, but it means a lot more if you had to drag yourself around Mount Gelmir's smoking caldera. It's embedded in my mind, every inch, every facet, every corpse in Caelid, every freestanding structure in Liurnia...and yet despite how much I know, there's still so much I missed. It took me a year to find out about Albinauric pots, and I only looked it up because I got smacked by one when I was invading! Fromsoft has never been afraid to just hide things from the player; these games are utterly indifferent about whether or not you find every single item or every nook and every cranny and it makes me wish more titles were willing to just let the player miss things. I had a friend who had no idea there was an entire sector, a massive drop by an NPC just barely hidden; a huge chunk of a necropolis you can only visit towards the endgame. There are maybe a few complaints to be made about how the combat is put together (and there are degenerate playstyles out there, but that's kind of inevitable in a game with this much breadth), but I still think it's by far some of the best that Fromsoft has made. I would argue it's even better than Bloodborne's combat loop, partially because you don't have to hunt for vials, partially because there's just more variety. I won't go into the boss fights, mostly because you will know how Fromsoft's combat rhythm is if you play any of the other games. I would go so far as to say this is probably fromsoft's best boss lineup in a base game. If that sounds like hearsay, do keep in mind that even DS3 had way less consistency in boss quality, DS2's base lineup is truly terrible, and DS1 had both bosses that were kind of jank and a lot who were just...not very good. That's not even getting into DeS' lineup which is truly rough after 15 years of iteration. ER doesn't share that problem in its main lineup. Like, frankly the remembrance bosses, several of the optional fights, are all pretty consistently interesting to fight (save some truly insufferable lingering hitboxes. Looking at you, Fallingstar Beast.) Elden Ring is three Dark Souls games stapled together, laid in a map with combat that takes queues from Sekiro and build variety that even exceeds DS2. It says a lot that even now, a year into this game's life cycle, I am still getting invades. I mean I'm not exactly going to convince anyone who wasn't already looking at this game and I'm not really gonna be swayed by discourse because I've had a long, long time to percolate my thoughts. ER good, actually. Basically.

Ah, Elden Ring, the game that's so easy even a blindfolded monkey with one hand tied behind its back could beat it. I mean, sure, the bosses are giant, imposing monsters that will make you feel like an ant in comparison, but once you figure out their weak points, they're about as threatening as a kitten with a ball of yarn. And those open-world areas? Please. Who needs a map or a compass when you can just wander aimlessly and stumble upon all the hidden secrets and treasures without breaking a sweat? And don't even get me started on the combat. It's like the game is playing itself. Just mash some buttons and watch as your character effortlessly decimates everything in its path. Sure, you might die a few times, but that's just to give you a false sense of challenge. The truth is, this game is about as difficult as a Sunday crossword puzzle. So if you're looking for a game that's so easy it's practically a walk in the park, then Elden Ring is the game for you. Just don't forget to bring a picnic basket and a frisbee, because you'll have plenty of time to enjoy the scenery.
